anchor: CBN and the institutional architecture of drug-law enforcement
argumentsAgainst: Enforcement-led approaches can be insufficient if demand reduction, rehabilitation and livelihood alternatives do not receive comparable attention.
Source-level eradication may affect vulnerable cultivators unless accompanied by lawful and sustainable livelihood transitions.
argumentsFor: A specialised agency can combine regulation of licit opium cultivation with action against illicit cultivation, trafficking and precursor diversion.
Digital governance, intelligence-led operations and youth-focused interventions can improve coordination between enforcement and prevention.

indiaImplications: Drug trafficking is an internal-security concern because transnational networks can exploit pharmaceutical diversion, precursor supply chains and border-linked distribution channels.
A coordinated model linking enforcement, digital systems, public outreach and alternative livelihoods can strengthen both supply reduction and social resilience.
Youth-focused prevention can connect narcotics control with public health, education and community-based intervention rather than relying only on punitive action.

mainsPractice.stem: Discuss how a specialised narcotics agency can integrate regulatory functions, intelligence-led enforcement and social prevention to address drug trafficking in India.

officialFacts.text: Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) celebrates 77th Foundation Day and reaffirms India’s vision for a “Nasha Mukt Yuva for Viksit Bharat”, through intensified enforcement, digital governance, and mission “Yuva Raksha”.

example.heading: Illustration
example.text: Suppose intelligence inputs indicate diversion of a controlled pharmaceutical from a lawful supply chain. A coordinated response could combine regulatory verification, investigation of the trafficking network, seizure under applicable law and prevention support for affected communities. This is a hypothetical illustration, not a reported event.

pocketRead.excerpt: CBN’s 77th Foundation Day highlights an integrated narcotics-control approach combining enforcement, digital governance and youth-focused prevention.

question.answer: An integrated approach is preferable: regulation can prevent diversion, intelligence can disrupt trafficking, and youth-focused prevention can reduce vulnerability. Enforcement should be paired with rehabilitation, community participation and lawful livelihood options so that supply control does not become socially counterproductive.
question.prompt: Why should narcotics control combine enforcement with prevention and livelihood support?

sections.heading: Institutional role
paragraphs: CBN is described as a specialised agency under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, with responsibilities spanning licit opium-poppy cultivation, narcotics trade oversight and intelligence-led enforcement under the NDPS Act, 1985.

sections.heading: Integrated response
paragraphs: The source title links intensified enforcement with digital governance and Mission “Yuva Raksha”. The policy lesson is that supply reduction and youth protection should operate together; enforcement alone cannot substitute for prevention, rehabilitation or lawful livelihood support.

Use digital systems for traceability, intelligence analysis and case monitoring with safeguards against misuse and protection of lawful data rights.
Pair illicit-crop control and trafficking disruption with rehabilitation, community participation and viable lawful livelihoods.
Evaluate youth-focused interventions through measurable prevention and treatment outcomes, not only seizure or arrest figures.
